query: My doctor found a kidney stone. How do they get rid of it?
final_answer: If a stone will not pass on its own, doctors can use shock waves to break it into smaller pieces [1]. Doctors may insert a scope through the urethra to reach the stone [1]. For larger stones or those that block urine flow, surgery such as percutaneous nephrolithotomy can be performed to take the stone out [3]. The specific treatment chosen depends on the stone’s size, what it is made of, and whether it is causing symptoms or blockage [4].

query: Why would someone keep wheezing, coughing, and feel tightness in their chest?
final_answer: Wheezing, coughing, and chest tightness are common symptoms of acute bronchitis, which often follows a cold or flu and may last for weeks [1]. Chronic bronchitis includes coughing, wheezing, and chest discomfort [1]. Chronic bronchitis is a long‑term condition that keeps coming back or never goes away completely [2]. Chronic bronchitis is frequently caused by long‑term exposure to cigarette smoke or other air pollutants [2]. Asthma can cause coughing, wheezing, chest tightness, and shortness of breath, and these symptoms may vary over time [3].

query: What tests do doctors use to check for Alzheimer's?
final_answer: Doctors may ask about overall health, past medical problems, ability to carry out daily activities, and changes in behavior and personality [1]. They conduct tests that measure memory, problem‑solving, attention, counting, and language skills [1]. Standard medical tests such as blood and urine tests are also performed to help rule out other possible causes [1]. Brain scans are used to look for anything in the brain that does not look normal [1].

final_answer: Most cases of Prader‑Willi syndrome are not inherited, especially when caused by a deletion of the paternal chromosome 15 or by maternal uniparental disomy. [1] These genetic changes occur as random events during the formation of reproductive cells or early embryonic development, so affected individuals usually have no family history of the disorder. [1] In rare instances a genetic change that inactivates genes on the paternal chromosome 15 can be passed from one generation to the next, making the condition inherited. [1] The risk to other family members depends on the specific genetic cause of the person’s Prader‑Willi syndrome. [2]

Huntington disease is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern, meaning one copy of the altered gene is enough to cause the disorder. [1] An affected person usually inherits the altered gene from an affected parent, although rare cases occur where a parent does not have the disorder. [1] When a person with Huntington disease has children, each child has a 50% chance of inheriting the mutated gene and developing the condition. [2] In rare instances, a new (de novo) mutation can cause Huntington disease in a person who does not inherit it from a parent. [2]

Crohn disease is linked to variations in several specific genes, including ATG16L1, IRGM, NOD2, and IL23R [1]. These gene variations affect proteins that are involved in immune system function and may disrupt the intestine’s normal response to bacteria [1]. Genetic risk regions have also been identified on chromosomes 5 and 10, such as the IBD5 locus on chromosome 5 and other “gene desert” areas that may regulate nearby genes [1]. The inheritance pattern is unclear because many genetic and environmental factors are likely involved, though the disease tends to cluster in families [2]. Researchers consider genes as one of the factors that may play a role in causing Crohn’s disease [3].

MELAS is caused by mutations in mitochondrial DNA and is transmitted by maternal (mitochondrial) inheritance [1]. Only egg cells contribute mitochondria to the embryo, so only females can pass the mutation to their children [1]. The disorder can appear in every generation of a family and can affect both males and females [1]. Most people with MELAS inherit an altered mitochondrial gene from their mother, although it can also arise from a new mutation without a family history [1].

query: What condition is linked to mutations in the DMD gene?
final_answer: Mutations in the DMD gene cause Duchenne muscular dystrophy, a rapidly progressive form of muscular dystrophy that primarily affects boys [1]. Mutations in the DMD gene also cause Becker muscular dystrophy, another form of muscular dystrophy [4]. Both Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophies are classified as dystrophinopathies because they result from faulty or missing dystrophin [4].

query: What condition is linked to mutations in the PAH gene?
final_answer: Mutations in the PAH gene cause phenylketonuria. [1] The PAH gene provides instructions for making the enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase. [1] When PAH gene mutations reduce the activity of phenylalanine hydroxylase, phenylalanine from the diet is not processed effectively and can build up to toxic levels in the blood and other tissues. [1] Classic PKU, the most severe form of the disorder, occurs when phenylalanine hydroxylase activity is severely reduced or absent. [1] Mutations in the PAH gene that allow the enzyme to retain some activity result in milder versions of this condition, such as variant PKU or non‑PKU hyperphenylalaninemia. [1]

query: What condition is linked to mutations in the TSC1 gene?
final_answer: Mutations in the TSC1 gene can cause tuberous sclerosis complex. [1] Mutations in the TSC1 gene can also cause lymphangioleiomyomatosis. [3] Renal oncocytomas can occur in people with tuberous sclerosis complex, which is caused by mutations in the TSC1 or TSC2 gene. [4]

query: What condition is linked to mutations in the ABCD1 gene?
final_answer: Mutations in the ABCD1 gene cause X‑linked adrenoleukodystrophy. [1] The disorder is inherited in an X‑linked pattern because the ABCD1 gene is located on the X chromosome. [3] In males, one altered copy of the ABCD1 gene is sufficient to cause the disease, while females usually develop milder or later‑onset symptoms. [3]
